attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own August 2026 post.

semantics.note: The normalised wording keeps the meaning: OpenAI used evasive legal language instead of truly ruling out surveillance of US citizens for the government. It is a past-tense observation.

contract.note: The contract fairly separates a public commitment from a legally complete exclusion, and treats 'mealy mouth' as criticism. The result depends on whether a qualified prohibition counts as refusing to opt out. The evidence only covers the Pentagon deal, not the whole US government.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure from March 2, 2026. It publicly added a ban on intentional domestic surveillance of US persons, which cuts against a flat refusal to opt out. It is a company statement, and the full contract terms are not shown.

The Atlantic, reproduced by the AI Incident Database. Outside legal experts say words like 'intentionally' and 'deliberate' leave room for incidental or automated surveillance, and OpenAI gave no definitions. They also say the change is meaningfully different, so this support is only partial.

reviews.rationale: Part of the claim fails: OpenAI did adopt an express, public ban on intentional domestic surveillance in its Pentagon deal, so a flat refusal to opt out is contradicted. Part holds: the qualified wording ('intentionally', 'deliberate', undefined terms) leaves gaps that experts flagged, which fits the 'legalese' criticism. Nothing shows any coverage beyond the Pentagon, or deliberate evasion.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. The layout suggests the line first appeared in his November 2024 quote-tweet, which he republished approvingly in the August 2026 post.

semantics.note: The normalised wording keeps 'virtually every' and the unspecified 'several years'. It is a firm self-assessment of his past record.

contract.note: The plain reading (almost all distinct warnings borne out) is ordinary. The line may date from 2024, but because Marcus republished it in the 2026 post, the August 20, 2026 cutoff is defensible. Requiring a complete audit with duplicates removed is strict but fair.

evidence.note: An unverified, LLM-scored dataset of Marcus's Substack posts with a March 2026 cutoff. It is not an independent, complete audit for this period and cannot settle the claim.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no complete list of Marcus's warnings and no independent check of their outcomes up to August 2026. The only item is unverified context, so the evidence cannot settle whether almost all of his warnings came true.

attribution.note: The device-building part is attributed to reports ('reportedly'). The uploading part ('no doubt') is Marcus's own assertion, and the drafter attributes the two parts correctly.

semantics.note: The normalised wording keeps 'reportedly' and 'no doubt' separate. 'No doubt' is high confidence, not a hedge, so the uploading claim can be scored. 'They' most plausibly means OpenAI.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair: devices meant for continuous monitoring that send all captured speech to the cloud. The evaluator chose the August 2026 reporting window but flagged that choice. Requiring technical evidence for the claim about all speech is appropriate.

evidence.note: Bloomberg reporting via the LA Times, August 2026, within the target period. It describes a speaker meant for use throughout the day, with microphones, a camera, and listening lights. Nothing shows continuous monitoring or uploading of all speech.
MacRumors, February 2026, outside the target period. It says the speaker is designed to observe users and learn about them, but does not show that all speech is sent to the cloud.

reviews.rationale: Reports show OpenAI developing a sensor-equipped speaker meant for all-day use. But nothing in the packet shows continuous monitoring or that everything users say is uploaded to the cloud, and nothing establishes the opposite either. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own November 2024 tweet, republished approvingly in his August 2026 post.

semantics.note: A firm claim that 24/7 surveillance is the only route to profitable generative AI for Microsoft and OpenAI. Classing it as causal is reasonable.

contract.note: Reading it as surveillance being necessary for generative-AI profit is fair. The contradiction test (either company profitable without surveillance) fits the 'only one play' wording. The contract correctly refuses to fill in a missing accounting basis.

evidence.note: Microsoft's consolidated results for the quarter ending June 2026 (company disclosure). It does not separate out generative-AI profit or link it to any data practices.

reviews.rationale: No evidence separates generative-AI profitability at either company or ties it to surveillance practices. Company-wide earnings cannot show whether surveillance is necessary, so the packet does not settle the claim.
